newsitem.title: UK: Continental denounces UK's BA/AA study.
newsitem.headline: Continental denounces UK's BA/AA study.

text.p: A senior executive of Continental Airlines Inc on Thursday described a British competition review of the controversial alliance plan between British Airways Plc and American Airlines as "morally corrupt". Barry Simon, senior vice president in charge of international operations at Continental, made the comments in London in reference to a report by the UK Deparment of Trade and Industry and competition watchdog the Office of Fair Trading.
"I think this is a really corrupt process -- an intellectually and morally corrupt process," Simon said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.

Simon also criticised the OFT at a news conference in London where he said conditions proposed by the OFT for approving the BA/American deal would not enable rival airlines to mount effective transatlantic competition at London Heathrow.

Continental and other airlines have until tomorrow to make representations to the OFT on British proposals to conditionally approve the alliance provided BA and American release 168 weekly takeoff and landing slots at London Heathrow.
Simon said the OFT slots proposal was inadequate and the OFT had failed to take account of the need for rivals to be guaranteed access to ground facilities at Heathrow.
"It is inconceivable that any serious report would have failed to consider that," he told journalists.

He also said that the 168 slots BA and American had been asked to release were insufficient, especially if they were parcelled out to several different airlines, which would dilute the effectiveness of such a measure.
"BA would much rather confront a whole bunch of pygmies than one or two substantial competitors," he said.
Simon said Continental could provide effective competition on the London-New York market if it was given Heathrow slots and ground facilities for six daily services to Newark.

He said altogether Continental would be asking the OFT this week for for 140 weekly slots at Heathrow which would allow it both to develop Newark as a rival to JFK for the all-important Heathrow market and to start a Heathrow-Houston service to counter BA and American's threatened London-Dallas monopoly.
Continental was also calling for BA and American to be compelled to give up Heathrow slots for free rather than be allowed to sell them to the highest bidder.

UK general manager Mike Carter said it was possible that BA might be able to sell Heathrow slots for 1.5 million stg apiece because of its attraction as London's most popular airport, particularly for lucrative transatlantic business traffic.
"If BA were to enjoy this windfall profit....They would have a huge war chest to reinforce their dominance," he told the news conference.
